The New York Times reported that 38 people watched Kitty Genovese be stabbed to death in 1964 and did nothing — the story that founded an entire field of “bystander effect” research. Decades of investigation later found most of the 38 weren’t eyewitnesses at all, and none could have seen the whole attack from where they stood | The Long View, ScienceBlog

For more than half a century, introductory psychology courses have opened their unit on helping behaviour with the same story: in Queens, New York, in 1964, thirty-eight people watched a woman get stabbed to death and none of them did anything. The story is real in the sense that a woman was murdered and that a newspaper printed those numbers. Almost everything else about how it’s usually told has turned out to be wrong.

What the original story actually claimed

Catherine “Kitty” Genovese, a 28-year-old bar manager, was attacked and stabbed by Winston Moseley outside her apartment building in Kew Gardens in the early hours of 13 March 1964, in two separate assaults about ten minutes apart, in an episode that spanned roughly half an hour from the first attack to her death; she was raped during the second, fatal attack. Two weeks later, New York Times reporter Martin Gansberg published a story under the headline “37 Who Saw Murder Didn’t Call the Police,” though the article’s own opening line gave a different number: “38 respectable, law-abiding citizens in Queens watched a killer stalk and stab a woman” — for more than half an hour, the article said, in three separate attacks.

That inconsistency, 37 in the headline, 38 in the text, has sat unremarked in the historical record for decades; it’s the 38 figure that stuck, becoming the number cited in psychology textbooks and by the researchers who built a field around it.

Social psychologists Bibb Latané and John Darley read the Gansberg account and used it as the motivating case for what became the bystander effect: the finding, developed through their own separate experiments beginning in 1968, that people are less likely to help in an emergency when they believe other bystanders are present, because responsibility for acting feels diffused across the group. Their experimental work on diffusion of responsibility is real, replicated, and remains a legitimate part of social psychology. The Genovese case was the anecdote that opened the door to it, not itself a piece of that experimental evidence.

What later investigation actually found

The most thorough published reassessment is Rachel Manning, Mark Levine and Alan Collins’s 2007 paper in American Psychologist, “The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping: The parable of the 38 witnesses.” Working from trial records, police files and contemporary reporting, they concluded there is no evidence that 38 people watched the murder, no evidence that those who were aware of it saw the attack itself, and no evidence that witness inaction caused her death. They frame the story explicitly as a parable, something taught for its moral clarity rather than for its accuracy, and note it had been repeated uncritically in psychology curricula for decades.

Journalist Kevin Cook went further in his 2014 book on the case, working from police files, trial transcripts and interviews with people involved. His account puts the actual police tally at 49 people who reported seeing or hearing something that night, of whom perhaps a dozen or so could reasonably be called eyewitnesses to any part of the events, a figure that varies somewhat depending on which secondary account is consulted, but is consistently far below “38 witnesses to a murder.” The “38” figure itself appears to have originated with a police tally passed to Commissioner Michael Murphy, who relayed it to Times editor A.M. Rosenthal.

The detail that undoes the story most completely, though, is architectural rather than statistical. The fatal second attack took place in an interior vestibule, out of view from the street and from most surrounding apartments. Investigators found no one who witnessed the entire attack from start to finish, because the geometry of the building made that impossible regardless of how many people were awake or watching from a window during the earlier, more visible portion of the assault.

What actually happened, according to the record

People did act, contrary to the story’s central image of collective paralysis. A neighbour, Robert Mozer, shouted from his window during the first attack and briefly drove Moseley off. A teenager who heard the commotion alerted his father, who called the police. Karl Ross called police later, though not in time. Sophia Farrar, a friend of Genovese’s who lived in the building, went down to her and stayed with her, holding her, before help arrived. The story that became the field’s founding case study left all of this out.

The bystander effect itself doesn’t need Kitty Genovese’s murder to be true; the diffusion-of-responsibility experiments Latané and Darley designed afterward stand on their own evidence, replicated many times since in controlled settings that have nothing to do with the original anecdote. The Genovese story mattered to that research programme mainly as a prompt, the question it made Latané and Darley want to test, not as data itself.

The story had consequences beyond psychology textbooks, too, some of them genuinely constructive. It’s frequently credited, alongside other factors, with helping build public and political support for a unified emergency telephone number in the United States, the system that became 911, on the logic that easier reporting might counter exactly the kind of hesitation the Genovese story seemed to describe. It’s a strange legacy for an account this inaccurate to have: real infrastructure and real research built partly on a version of events that didn’t happen the way it was told, even while the underlying human tendency the story was used to illustrate turned out to be genuine and well documented on its own separate terms.

What the case actually demonstrates, once the record is checked against the story, is a different and arguably more useful lesson about how a specific, memorable number in a newspaper headline can travel for sixty years largely unexamined, cited by people, including researchers, who had every professional reason to check it and mostly didn’t. A. M. Rosenthal, the Times editor who ran the original story, went on to write his own book the same year, Thirty-Eight Witnesses: The Kitty Genovese Case, which helped cement the 38-witness framing in the public imagination even further, at a moment when the more careful reconstruction that Manning, Levine and Collins would eventually publish was still four decades away.

神了，有人把Qwen模型训成了一个生图模型？？

有人干了个很抽象的实验：

直接拿 Qwen 做强化学习，让一个 Coding Model 学会用 JavaScript 画水彩画。

没有 Stable Diffusion，没有 Flux，也不是调用什么图片 API。

每一张图背后，真的是 Qwen 自己写出来的一段代码。

而且他们甚至给审美做了一套 Reward，让模型靠 RL 一轮轮学会怎样画得更好看。

具体流程是这样的⬇️

1️⃣先给 Qwen 一个 Prompt。
Qwen 根据要求写一段 p5.brush JavaScript，再把这段代码扔进浏览器环境里真正执行，渲染成图片。
2️⃣画完之后还没结束。
Judge 模型会继续看这张图，判断它有没有遵循 Prompt、构图怎么样、技法怎么样，以及最关键的这玩意到底好不好看。
3️⃣评分变成 Reward，再拿回去训练 Qwen。

于是一个本来拿来写代码的模型，就这么一点一点学会了画画。

这套东西最有意思的地方，其实是他们训练审美时踩的坑。

一开始团队搞了足足 9 个 Reward。

看起来很科学，代码质量、绘画技法、Prompt 遵循、审美各种维度全部覆盖。

结果 Reward 一路往上涨，画却越来越抽象。

很明显 Qwen 找到了捷径开始Hack这些Reward。

最后画出来的东西就开始疯狂收敛成差不多的五瓣小花。

后来他们才发现，很多 Judge 的判断高度相关。

换句话说，表面上有 9 个指标，实际上可能是在把同一种偏好重复奖励好几遍。

于是他们干脆大砍 Reward，只留下 4 个。

然后人肉看了 1664 张模型生成的作品，从中挑出自己真正觉得好看的图片，拿来当审美参考。

结果新的 Reward 设计，只用了原来大概 1/3 的训练步数，就追上了之前的效果，之后还能继续提升。

模型自己写画图代码也越来越熟练。

一度生成一张图要写到 13500 Token 左右，后来逐渐压到了 2000 Token 以下。

还有一个很典的 Prompt 工程事故。

一开始他们担心 Qwen 不熟悉 p5.brush，于是好心往 System Prompt 里塞了大约 400 行 API 文档。

结果模型学完之后，开始非常自信地发明根本不存在的 API。

最后团队干脆把几百行文档删掉，只明确告诉它可以用哪些核心方法。

结果反而正常了。

训练本身跑在 PrimeIntellect 上，Rollout 的图片渲染则放在 Modal 上。

当然，这条路线现在比直接调用生图模型慢得多，画面质量也不是为了跟 Flux 正面打。

但我觉得它真正有意思的是另一件事：

以前我们讲 AI 生图，基本都是Prompt → Image

这里却变成了Prompt → Code → Image

最后得到的不只是一张图，还有一整套可以继续修改、调参数、复用的生成逻辑。

今天是 p5.js 水彩画。

以后如果这套思路继续往 SVG、网页、Figma、3D、CAD 这些东西里走，就很有意思了。

AI 生成的可能不再只是最后那堆像素。

而是作品背后真正可编辑的结构。

RESPECT NEVER GOES OUT OF FASHION

Earlier today, I went for a friend’s mother’s burial.

I knew some old friends would be there,people I hadn’t seen in over 15 years. 
We had talked about seeing each other, but I gave the usual excuse:

“I’m not driving, so I probably won’t make it.”

Around 11:50am, one of them sent his driver to pick me up.

Two hours later, I arrived and was taken straight to the VIP section where they were all waiting.

Mehn… seeing old friends after 15 years? 🥹

It felt GOOD.

Then I sat down at the table.

In front of me was a cold bottle of water.

I was thirsty, so I opened it and almost finished it without thinking twice.

About 10 minutes later, my friend’s mother walked to the table and asked:

“Who took my water?”

Everyone at the table had a bottle, but theirs were already open because they had just finished eating.

Mine was the only unopened one.

I immediately felt bad.

I turned to her, held her hands and said:

“Mummy, I took your water. 
I didn’t know it was yours.”

She looked at me and said:

“My daughter, don’t worry. 
Drink it, you hear?”

Just like that…

The anger disappeared.

And it reminded me of something we must never lose:

RESPECT.

Our mothers and fathers may not understand all our technology.

They may not know what AI is.

They may not understand Web3, crypto, or whatever new thing the world is talking about, e no really concern them.

But they understand something deeply:

Respect.

Imagine I had responded to her like a 21st-century, AI-tech-savvy Queen:

“Ma, it was an honest mistake. There was no indication that the water belonged to you.”

😂😂😂

That conversation might have become a TED Talk.

Sometimes, wisdom is knowing, understanding and deploying Culture quotient (CQ)not just IQ.

You can be educated.

You can be successful.

You can be technologically advanced.

You can speak the finest English in the room.

But when you stand before an elder, humility will always take you further than intelligence.

We are moving forward as a generation.

Let’s embrace technology.

Let’s challenge old ideas.

Let’s build new systems.

But let’s not throw away the values that built us.

Respect for elders is not old-fashioned.

It is part of who we are.

And some things are worth carrying into the future. ❤️
